title: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
learningObjective: Describe infrastructure, platform and software as a service, what you manage in each, and choose the right one for a use case.
foundation: IaaS (infrastructure as a service): you rent the raw building blocks (virtual machines, storage, networks) and manage the operating system and everything on it. Most control, most work.
PaaS (platform as a service): you bring your application and data; Azure runs the platform (OS, runtime, patching, scaling). Less control, much less maintenance.
SaaS (software as a service): you use a finished application over the internet (email, CRM). You manage your data, users and settings only.
Pizza analogy: IaaS is buying ingredients and cooking in a rented kitchen, PaaS is take-and-bake, SaaS is eating at the restaurant.
engineer: IaaS: Azure Virtual Machines, Virtual Network, managed disks. You handle OS updates, middleware, runtime, security configuration and backups. Use cases: lift-and-shift migration, test and development, custom software needing OS access, storage and backup infrastructure.

PaaS: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, Azure Functions, Azure Kubernetes Service (managed control plane), Azure Cosmos DB. Microsoft handles OS, patching, runtime and often high availability. Use cases: development frameworks (build apps without managing infrastructure), analytics and business intelligence, APIs.
SaaS: Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Microsoft Teams. The provider manages the application. Use cases: email and messaging, business productivity, finance and expense tracking.

Shared responsibility by type: IaaS customer manages OS, network controls, applications, identity infrastructure, data; PaaS shares applications, network controls and identity infrastructure; SaaS customer keeps data, devices, accounts, identities.

Trade-offs: IaaS offers maximum flexibility and control but requires the most management. PaaS speeds development but limits OS-level customisation. SaaS has the least effort but the least customisation.
Choosing: needs OS control or installed agents → IaaS. Want to deploy code without servers → PaaS. Need a ready-made business application → SaaS.

example.title: One company, three service types
body: Contoso migrates a legacy inventory app that needs a specific Windows agent to Azure VMs (IaaS).
Its new customer portal runs on App Service with Azure SQL Database (PaaS), and staff use Microsoft 365 for email and Teams (SaaS).

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources

troubleshooting.symptom: A PaaS app needs a custom OS driver.
Too much time spent patching VMs that host a simple website.
troubleshooting.fix: Move the site to App Service.

comparisons.difference: Often treated as a middle ground: package the app with dependencies; run on PaaS services such as Container Apps or AKS.
Serverless is commonly grouped with PaaS; it adds per-execution billing and scale to zero.

misconceptions.myth: SaaS means the provider owns your data.
misconceptions.reality: You always own and are responsible for your data.

misconceptions.myth: PaaS gives no control at all.
misconceptions.reality: You control the application, its settings and scaling.
Management effort is a cost too.

architectureDecisions: Prefer SaaS, then PaaS, then IaaS, unless requirements need more control.
Use IaaS for lift-and-shift, then modernise to PaaS.
